events.what: One of Africa's earliest peaceful transfers of power by election, and stable ever since.

culture.label: Morna
culture.text: Melancholy song built around sodade — longing for what is far away; UNESCO-listed.

culture.label: Diaspora
culture.text: More Cape Verdeans live abroad than at home, especially in the US, Portugal and the Netherlands.

culture.label: Cachupa
culture.text: Slow-cooked corn and beans, eaten fried for breakfast the next morning.

culture.label: Kriolu
culture.text: The everyday language, with distinct island varieties; Portuguese is for official use.

culture.label: Fogo
culture.text: An active volcano with vineyards inside the caldera and villages that keep rebuilding.

talkAbout: Island differences — each one claims a distinct character.
avoid: Water scarcity and emigration are constant pressures. Don't treat Kriolu as broken Portuguese.

people.name: Said Mohamed Cheikh
people.why: A doctor who became the islands' first head of government under French rule.

people.name: Ahmed Abdallah
people.why: Declared independence in 1975 and was twice removed by mercenaries before being killed.

people.name: Nawal Soilihi
people.why: Sings in Comorian and blends Sufi devotional song with the gambusi lute.

people.name: Salim Ali Amir
people.why: The most popular Comorian musician of his generation, and a social commentator.

people.name: Mohamed Youssouf
people.why: Part of the side that reached the Africa Cup of Nations knockout stage in 2022 on its debut.

events.title: The Swahili coast
events.what: The islands were part of the Indian Ocean trading world, with Shirazi and Arab settlement.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Three islands left France; Mayotte voted to stay and remains French.

events.title: The coup years
events.what: Around twenty coups or attempts, several involving the French mercenary Bob Denard.

events.title: The Africa Cup of Nations
events.what: The Coelacanths reached the last sixteen on their first appearance, with an outfield player in goal.

culture.label: Ylang-ylang
culture.text: The Comoros grows most of the world's supply of the flower behind many classic perfumes.

culture.label: Grand mariage
culture.text: An elaborate and expensive wedding that confers full adult social status; families save for years.

culture.label: Coelacanth
culture.text: The 'living fossil' fish, thought extinct for 65 million years, was rediscovered in these waters.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Langouste à la vanille, and rice with coconut and cardamom.

culture.label: Karthala
culture.text: One of the world's largest active craters, on Grande Comore.

avoid: Mayotte's status and migration by boat to it are painful subjects. Political instability is a sore point.

people.name: Marien Ngouabi
people.why: Declared the People's Republic of the Congo and was assassinated in office.

people.name: Alain Mabanckou
people.why: One of the most acclaimed Francophone writers alive, and a Prix Renaudot winner.

people.name: Sony Labou Tansi
people.why: A playwright and novelist whose work is central to modern African literature in French.

people.name: Zao
people.why: 'Ancien Combattant' became one of Africa's best-known anti-war songs.

people.name: Emmanuel Dongala
people.why: A professor of chemistry who became one of Congo's leading novelists.

events.title: Brazza's treaty
events.what: Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed with the Téké king; Brazzaville is named after him.

events.title: Capital of Free France
events.what: Brazzaville served as the symbolic capital of Free France during the occupation.

events.title: Independence
events.what: The Republic of the Congo left French rule.

events.title: The civil war
events.what: A conflict between militias devastated Brazzaville and returned Sassou Nguesso to power.

culture.label: La Sape
culture.text: The dandy society of elegant dressers began in Brazzaville and Kinshasa alike.

culture.label: Rumba
culture.text: Congolese rumba is shared with the DRC and jointly UNESCO-listed.

culture.label: Odzala
culture.text: Rainforest national parks with forest elephants and western lowland gorillas.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Saka-saka cassava leaves, grilled river fish and fufu.

culture.label: Two capitals
culture.text: Brazzaville faces Kinshasa across the river — the closest pair of capitals in the world.

avoid: Sassou Nguesso's decades in power and the civil war are politically charged. Don't confuse this Congo with the DRC.

people.name: Francisco Macías Nguema
people.why: His eleven-year rule killed or exiled perhaps a third of the population.

people.name: Donato Ndongo-Bidyogo
people.why: Equatorial Guinea's foremost novelist and historian, writing in Spanish from exile.

people.name: María Nsué Angüe
people.why: Wrote the country's first novel by a woman, Ekomo.

people.name: Emilio Nsue
people.why: Top scorer at the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations, when Equatorial Guinea beat Ivory Coast 4–0.

people.name: Leoncio Evita
people.why: Wrote what is generally considered the first novel by a Black author in Spanish Guinea.

events.title: Spanish Guinea
events.what: Portugal ceded the territory to Spain, making it Africa's only Spanish-speaking colony.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Equatorial Guinea left Spanish rule, and within months began eleven years of terror.

events.title: The coup
events.what: Teodoro Obiang deposed his uncle and has ruled ever since — the world's longest-serving living head of state.

events.title: Offshore oil
events.what: Large finds made it one of Africa's highest per-head incomes, with little of it reaching most people.

culture.label: Spanish
culture.text: The only sovereign African country where Spanish is official, alongside French and Portuguese.

culture.label: Bioko
culture.text: The capital sits on a volcanic island 40 km from Cameroon, while most territory is on the mainland.

culture.label: Balele
culture.text: Bubi and Fang dance traditions performed at community celebrations.

culture.label: Turtles
culture.text: Bioko's southern beaches are among the most important sea turtle nesting sites in Africa.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Succotash, pepper soup and plenty of fish and plantain.

talkAbout: Speaking Spanish in Africa, which surprises everyone.
Bioko's wildlife and the turtle beaches.
Football and the 2023 Cup of Nations.
avoid: Politics is genuinely dangerous. Oil wealth, corruption cases abroad and the Macías years are all off-limits in public.

people.name: Sobhuza II
people.why: Reigned for 82 years, the longest precisely dated reign of any monarch in history.

people.name: Mswati III
people.why: Crowned at eighteen; Africa's last absolute monarch, who renamed the country in 2018.

people.name: Sarah Mkhonza
people.why: A novelist and columnist who went into exile after writing about the monarchy.

people.name: Bhekithemba Dlamini
people.why: Part of the gospel and traditional music scene that dominates Eswatini's airwaves.

people.name: Sibusiso Dlamini
people.why: Served three separate terms as head of government across three decades.

events.title: The Swazi nation forms
events.what: The Dlamini dynasty consolidated a kingdom between the Zulu and the Boers.

events.title: British protectorate
events.what: Britain administered Swaziland, which kept its monarchy throughout.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Swaziland became independent with Sobhuza II as king.

events.title: Renamed Eswatini
events.what: Mswati III renamed the country on its fiftieth independence anniversary, partly to stop the confusion with Switzerland.

culture.label: Umhlanga
culture.text: The reed dance draws tens of thousands of young women each August in one of Africa's largest ceremonies.

culture.label: Incwala
culture.text: The kingship ceremony, the most sacred event of the year, lasting several weeks.

culture.label: Landscape
culture.text: A small country of four distinct climate zones, from highveld to lowveld.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Sidvudvu pumpkin porridge, and emasi soured milk with maize meal.

culture.label: Handicraft
culture.text: Candles, glass and woven goods from Ngwenya and Malkerns are exported worldwide.

avoid: The monarchy is above criticism in public, and the 2021 pro-democracy protests were violently suppressed. HIV prevalence is the world's highest and is a serious subject.

people.name: Amílcar Cabral
people.why: An agronomist who led the liberation war and wrote some of Africa's most influential political theory.

people.name: Luís Cabral
people.why: Amílcar's half-brother and independent Guinea-Bissau's first president.

people.name: Manecas Costa
people.why: Took gumbé music to international audiences.

people.name: Abdulai Sila
people.why: Wrote the country's first novel, and is its best-known writer.

people.name: Éder Fernandes
people.why: Bissau-Guinean-born, he scored the goal that won Portugal the 2016 European Championship.

events.title: Portuguese Guinea
events.what: Five centuries of Portuguese presence, concentrated on the coast and the slave trade.

events.title: The liberation war
events.what: PAIGC's guerrilla campaign was so effective it helped topple Portugal's own dictatorship.

events.title: Cabral assassinated
events.what: Killed months before independence he had spent his life fighting for.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Portugal recognised Guinea-Bissau after the Carnation Revolution.

culture.label: Bijagós
culture.text: An archipelago of 88 islands, matrilineal in custom, where women choose their husbands.

culture.label: Gumbé
culture.text: A polyrhythmic style that fuses the country's many ethnic musical traditions.

culture.label: Kriol
culture.text: Guinea-Bissau Creole is the shared language across more than twenty ethnic groups.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Rice with palm oil, jollof-style caldo, and plenty of fish and cashew.

culture.label: Cashews
culture.text: The dominant export, and the reason much of the rural economy rises and falls with one price.

talkAbout: The Bijagós islands and their matrilineal customs.
Cabral's writing, which is still studied.
avoid: Repeated coups and the drug-transit trade are sensitive. Politics has been unstable for decades.

people.name: Moshoeshoe I
people.why: Founded the Basotho nation by diplomacy as much as war, and secured British protection to survive.

people.name: Thomas Mofolo
people.why: Chaka is one of the great African novels, written in Sesotho in 1910.

people.name: Mpho 'M'atsepo Nthunya
people.why: Singing Away the Hunger gave a rare first-person account of rural Basotho women's lives.

people.name: Ntsu Mokhehle
people.why: A long-time opposition leader who eventually led the country in the 1990s.

people.name: Tšepo Tshola
people.why: The Village Pope, whose voice was known across southern Africa.

events.title: The nation forms
events.what: Moshoeshoe gathered refugees from the Difaqane wars at his mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu.

events.title: British protection
events.what: Moshoeshoe asked Queen Victoria for protection against the Boers, which is why Lesotho exists.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Basutoland became the Kingdom of Lesotho.

events.title: The Highlands Water Project
events.what: Dams began sending water to South Africa, becoming Lesotho's largest source of income.

culture.label: The blanket
culture.text: The Basotho blanket, worn pinned at the shoulder, carries patterns that signal status and occasion.

culture.label: Basotho pony
culture.text: A sure-footed mountain breed that is still the practical way to reach many villages.

culture.label: The Kingdom in the Sky
culture.text: The only country entirely above 1,000 m, with Africa's southernmost ski resort.

culture.label: Mokorotlo
culture.text: The conical straw hat on the national flag, modelled on a mountain near Thaba Bosiu.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Papa with moroho greens, and sesotho beer brewed from sorghum.

talkAbout: The blanket and what the patterns mean.
avoid: Political instability, migrant labour in South African mines and HIV prevalence are all difficult topics.

people.name: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf
people.why: Africa's first elected woman head of state, and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate.

people.name: Leymah Gbowee
people.why: Led the women's movement that helped end the civil war; shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize.

people.name: George Weah
people.why: The only African to win the Ballon d'Or, and later president of his country.

people.name: Joseph Jenkins Roberts
people.why: Born free in Virginia, he became Liberia's first president in 1848.

people.name: Angie Brooks
people.why: The first African woman to preside over the UN General Assembly.

events.title: The settlement
events.what: Freed and free-born African Americans settled at Cape Mesurado, creating a colony that became a country.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Liberia declared independence, becoming Africa's first republic.

events.title: The civil wars
events.what: Two wars killed around 250,000 people and displaced most of the country.

events.title: Two Nobel Prizes
events.what: Sirleaf and Gbowee shared the Peace Prize for women's role in ending the war.

culture.label: American echoes
culture.text: The flag has one star and eleven stripes, the capital is named for a US president, and the dollar is the currency.

culture.label: Liberian English
culture.text: A distinct variety with its own rhythm and vocabulary, spoken alongside about thirty languages.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Jollof, palm butter, and cassava leaf with rice — rice is the meal, everything else is 'soup'.

culture.label: Poro and Sande
culture.text: Initiation societies that structure village life and have their own masked figures.

culture.label: Football
culture.text: Weah is a national hero twice over, and the sport carried people through the war years.

talkAbout: George Weah, football and the Ballon d'Or.
avoid: The civil wars and Ebola are recent trauma. Tension between Americo-Liberian descendants and indigenous groups is a long-running fault line.

people.name: Moktar Ould Daddah
people.why: Mauritania's first president, who led it to independence and governed for eighteen years.

people.name: Dimi Mint Abba
people.why: A griot who became Mauritania's most celebrated musician and played the ardin harp.

people.name: Biram Dah Abeid
people.why: Born to a family of freed slaves, he has been repeatedly imprisoned for campaigning against slavery.

people.name: Mbarek Ould Beyrouk
people.why: The first Mauritanian to win the Ahmadou Kourouma Prize.

people.name: Mohamedou Ould Slahi
people.why: Held at Guantánamo for fourteen years without charge; his diary became an international bestseller.

events.title: The Almoravids
events.what: A movement from the western Sahara that came to rule Morocco and much of Spain.

events.title: Chinguetti
events.what: A caravan and scholarly city whose libraries of manuscripts survive in the desert.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Mauritania left French rule.

events.title: Abolishing slavery
events.what: The last country in the world to formally abolish it; it was only made a crime in 2007.

culture.label: The iron ore train
culture.text: Over two kilometres long, crossing the Sahara; locals ride free on top of the ore.

culture.label: Desert libraries
culture.text: Chinguetti's family libraries hold medieval manuscripts on law, astronomy and mathematics.

culture.label: Three teas
culture.text: Green tea poured three times, each sweeter than the last: bitter as life, sweet as love, gentle as death.

culture.label: Ardin
culture.text: A harp played only by women, at the centre of Moorish griot music.

culture.label: Banc d'Arguin
culture.text: A World Heritage coast where millions of migratory birds gather, fished by Imraguen using dolphins to herd fish.

talkAbout: The iron ore train, which fascinates travellers.
avoid: Slavery's persistence in practice, and racial hierarchy between Arab-Berber and Black Mauritanian communities, are serious and politically fraught.

people.name: Seewoosagur Ramgoolam
people.why: Led Mauritius to independence and is regarded as the father of the nation.

people.name: Ananda Devi
people.why: One of the most acclaimed Francophone writers of her generation.

people.name: Kaya
people.why: Created seggae by fusing séga and reggae; his death in police custody sparked riots.

people.name: J. M. G. Le Clézio
people.why: A Nobel laureate who holds Mauritian citizenship and writes often about the island.

people.name: Malcolm de Chazal
people.why: His aphorisms in Sens-Plastique were championed by the French surrealists.

events.title: The Dutch and the dodo
events.what: Dutch settlement drove the dodo to extinction within a century of first contact.

events.title: Isle de France
events.what: French rule brought sugar plantations and enslaved labour from Africa and Madagascar.

events.title: Abolition and indenture
events.what: After slavery ended, nearly half a million indentured workers arrived from India.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Mauritius left British rule and became a republic in 1992.

culture.label: Plural society
culture.text: Hindu, Muslim, Christian and Chinese communities, with public holidays for all of them.

culture.label: Séga
culture.text: Music and dance descended from enslaved people's gatherings, played on the ravanne drum; UNESCO-listed.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Dholl puri from a street cart, plus Creole rougaille, Chinese noodles and Indian curries.

culture.label: Aapravasi Ghat
culture.text: The immigration depot where indentured workers landed, now a World Heritage site.

culture.label: Kreol
culture.text: Mauritian Creole is what everyone speaks; English is for parliament and French for the press.

talkAbout: How so many communities share one small island.
avoid: The Chagos Islands dispute is a live national grievance. Communal politics is a delicate subject.

people.name: Manuel Pinto da Costa
people.why: Led the country to independence in 1975 and returned as elected president in 2011.

people.name: Alda Espírito Santo
people.why: Wrote the national anthem and was a leading voice of the independence movement.

people.name: Francisco José Tenreiro
people.why: A founder of Négritude in Portuguese, and the first to write it from these islands.

people.name: Conceição Lima
people.why: The country's leading contemporary poet, widely translated.

people.name: Olinda Beja
people.why: Writes about identity and belonging between São Tomé and Portugal.

events.title: Settlement
events.what: Uninhabited before the Portuguese arrived; the islands became the first plantation economy worked by enslaved Africans.

events.title: The chocolate islands
events.what: For a time São Tomé was the world's largest cocoa producer, worked under near-slavery conditions.

events.title: The Batepá massacre
events.what: Portuguese authorities killed hundreds of Forros; the date is now a national day of remembrance.

events.title: Independence
events.what: The islands left Portuguese rule after the Carnation Revolution.

culture.label: Cocoa
culture.text: Fine-flavour cocoa from old plantation estates is being revived by small producers.

culture.label: The equator
culture.text: It passes through the islet of Rolas, just off the southern tip of São Tomé.

culture.label: Tchiloli
culture.text: A centuries-old masked drama, a Portuguese play reworked with African performance over 400 years.

culture.label: Endemics
culture.text: Príncipe is a UNESCO biosphere reserve with birds found nowhere else on earth.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Calulu fish stew, breadfruit and plenty of tropical fruit.

talkAbout: Birdlife and the forests of Príncipe.
avoid: The plantation system and the Batepá massacre are painful history. The country is small and politics is personal.

people.name: James Mancham
people.why: Seychelles' first president, deposed a year later in a coup while abroad.

people.name: France-Albert René
people.why: Ruled for 27 years after the 1977 coup and built the welfare and education system.

people.name: Antoine Abel
people.why: The father of Seychellois literature, who wrote in Creole and French.

people.name: Danielle Jorre de St Jorre
people.why: Codified written Seychellois Creole and made it an official language.

people.name: Wavel Ramkalawan
people.why: An Anglican priest whose 2020 win was the country's first opposition victory since independence.

events.title: First settlement
events.what: The French settled uninhabited islands with planters and enslaved Africans.

events.title: British rule
events.what: Britain took the islands from France but left the French language and law largely in place.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Seychelles left British rule after 162 years.

events.title: Marine protection
events.what: Seychelles protected 30% of its ocean territory through a pioneering debt-for-nature swap.

culture.label: Coco de mer
culture.text: The largest seed in the plant kingdom, found only in the Vallée de Mai on Praslin.

culture.label: Tortoises
culture.text: Aldabra holds around 100,000 giant tortoises — more than the Galápagos.

culture.label: Three languages
culture.text: Seychellois Creole, English and French are all official, and most people use all three.

culture.label: Moutya
culture.text: A drum dance descended from enslaved people's gatherings, once banned; UNESCO-listed.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Grilled fish with Creole sauce, octopus curry and breadfruit chips.

talkAbout: The coco de mer and the Vallée de Mai.
avoid: The 1977 coup and one-party years still divide opinion. Small-island politics is intimate and gossip travels.

people.name: John Garang
people.why: Led the SPLA through the long war and signed the peace deal, dying in a helicopter crash weeks later.

people.name: Salva Kiir Mayardit
people.why: South Sudan's first and so far only president, recognisable by his black cowboy hat.

people.name: Emmanuel Jal
people.why: A former child soldier who became an international hip-hop artist and peace campaigner.

people.name: Alek Wek
people.why: A refugee from the war who became one of the most recognisable models in the world.

people.name: Manute Bol
people.why: One of the tallest men ever to play in the NBA, who gave most of his earnings to Sudanese causes.

events.title: The first civil war
events.what: Southern Sudanese fought Khartoum for seventeen years before an autonomy agreement.

events.title: The second civil war
events.what: Twenty-two years of war killed around two million people, mostly through famine and disease.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Almost 99% voted to secede, and South Sudan became the world's newest country.

events.title: Civil war again
events.what: A split between Kiir and Machar reignited conflict two years after independence.

culture.label: Cattle
culture.text: Among Dinka and Nuer communities cattle are wealth, bride price, poetry and identity.

culture.label: The Sudd
culture.text: One of the world's largest wetlands, where the White Nile spreads across a vast floodplain.

culture.label: Migration
culture.text: The white-eared kob migration rivals the Serengeti's in scale and is barely known abroad.

culture.label: Languages
culture.text: Over 60 languages; English is official and Juba Arabic is the everyday bridge.

culture.label: Music
culture.text: Dinka ox songs, composed by young men in praise of their favourite cattle.

talkAbout: The Sudd and the kob migration.
Independence in 2011, which people still remember celebrating.
avoid: The civil wars, famine and ethnic politics are current and devastating. Most South Sudanese abroad are refugees.

people.name: El-Ouali Mustapha Sayed
people.why: Founded the Polisario Front and was killed a few months after proclaiming the SADR.

people.name: Aminatou Haidar
people.why: Called the Sahrawi Gandhi for her non-violent campaigning; winner of the Right Livelihood Award.

people.name: Mariem Hassan
people.why: The best-known Sahrawi musician internationally, singing haul music of exile and resistance.

people.name: Mohamed Abdelaziz
people.why: Led the Polisario Front and the SADR for 40 years, mostly from the refugee camps.

people.name: Bahia Awah
people.why: A leading figure of the Generación de la Amistad, Sahrawi poets writing in Spanish.

events.title: Spanish Sahara
events.what: Spain colonised the territory and held it until Franco's death.

events.title: The Green March
events.what: Morocco sent 350,000 civilians across the border as Spain withdrew; Sahrawis fled to Algeria.

events.title: The war
events.what: Polisario fought Morocco and Mauritania; Morocco built a 2,700 km sand wall across the desert.

events.title: The ceasefire
events.what: The UN brokered a ceasefire promising a referendum on self-determination, never held.

culture.label: Three teas
culture.text: The same three-round tea ritual as across the western Sahara, taking an hour or more.

culture.label: Tents
culture.text: The khaima tent remains the centre of Sahrawi family life, including in the Algerian camps.

culture.label: Melhfa
culture.text: The bright wrapped cloth worn by Sahrawi women, in colours that identify the wearer's mood and occasion.

culture.label: Haul
culture.text: Desert blues on the tidinit lute, often carrying political lyrics.

culture.label: Emptiness
culture.text: One of the least densely populated territories on earth, mostly hamada and dune.

talkAbout: Music and poetry, which carry the political story.
Life in the Tindouf camps, where families have now lived for fifty years.
avoid: Sovereignty is disputed and unresolved; Moroccans and Sahrawis describe the same events in incompatible terms. Take care whose account you are hearing.
